reasoning: The claim that monosodium glutamate (MSG) causes headaches, numbness, and other symptoms known as "Chinese restaurant syndrome" has been thoroughly debunked by rigorous scientific research. The concept originated from an anecdotal 1968 letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine, which spurred widespread public panic rather than peer-reviewed evidence. Subsequent rigorous, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have consistently failed to demonstrate a causal link between MSG consumed in normal dietary amounts and these symptoms, with participants reporting symptoms at comparable rates when given placebos. Major food safety and health authorities, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the World Health Organization (WHO), classify MSG as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS), noting that the human body metabolizes added MSG identically to naturally occurring glutamates found in foods like tomatoes and aged cheeses.
